product_scope: Food recognition, segmentation, portion/mass estimation, and nutrition calculation are separate tasks. A correct dish label does not reveal cooked mass, oil, sauce, recipe, or hidden ingredients.
supported_platforms: Evaluation should use phone RGB images on iOS/Android device cohorts, with optional depth/AR as a separate condition.
pricing: Accuracy work is a data/annotation/evaluation cost, not an inference API price. A consented weighed-meal set is more valuable than a large unmeasured photo set for nutrition claims.
popularity_signal: Benchmark and dataset adoption are stronger evidence than consumer star ratings for model selection.
recognition_behavior: Benchmark the full assistive flow: photo -> top-k candidates/masks -> user correction -> serving/recipe confirmation -> deterministic database nutrients.
identified_services: Not applicable; the evidence concerns datasets and models rather than a vendor attribution.
model_or_provider_confidence: Dataset facts and published benchmark values are high-confidence within their stated protocols; transfer to SuperNutrition's cuisines/devices is not guaranteed.
local_inference_evidence: Food-101 supports dish classification but has no mass/calorie labels. Nutrition5k has 5,006 plates with ingredient masses/nutrients but controlled California cafeteria capture and RGB-D/multi-view signals. MyFoodRepo-273 has 24,119 real-world images, 39,325 polygons, and 273 categories but no calorie/weight ground truth. FoodSAM reports segmentation results, not calorie accuracy.
portion_and_nutrition_method: Nutrition5k reported 26.1% mean-relative MAE for direct 2D calorie prediction and 16.5% for a volume-assisted pipeline; the 9.5% portion-independent result still depends on reliable mass information. These values should not be presented as phone-photo guarantees.
static_findings: No consumer APK static evidence can substitute for a ground-truth benchmark. Model assets and provider strings do not reveal accuracy or calibration.
reverse_engineering_limits: Random image splits leak plate/person/device context; all views/frames of a meal must stay in one split. Dataset taxonomy, cuisine, capture rig, and labels limit cross-product comparison.
candidate_models: Use a detector/segmenter for visible items and a classifier/retriever for food candidates. VLMs may add open-vocabulary candidates but must be calibrated/abstain. No generic VLM should be allowed to invent nutrition values.
mobile_runtime_support: Use the same evaluation harness across Core ML, LiteRT, ONNX Runtime Mobile, and cloud providers so accuracy and device cost are compared fairly.
device_requirements: Measure latency, peak RAM, battery/thermal impact, model download size, offline behavior, and accelerator fallback on a representative device matrix.
expected_food_inference_quality: Recommended metrics: top-1/top-5 recall, macro-F1, per-class recall, calibration; mask mAP/mAR and class-balanced mIoU; grams MAE/bias/90th percentile and within +/-20%; kcal/macros MAE and per-meal/per-day error; abstention/selective-risk curves; correction time and acceptance rate.
unit_cost_estimate: No single benchmark cost. Record annotation cost and cloud cost per image alongside accuracy; a cheaper model that causes extra user corrections may be more expensive at product level.
privacy_and_compliance: Food photos may expose faces, homes, locations, routines, and sensitive diet/health data. Obtain consent, strip metadata, minimize retention, support deletion/export, avoid allergy-safe or medical claims, and never use image estimates alone for insulin dosing.
recommendation: Build a consented, culturally diverse 300-500+ meal pilot with exact weights, recipes/brands, raw/cooked state, oil/sauce, device/cuisine/lighting slices, and person/restaurant/device/time-separated splits. Compare local-only, cloud-only, and hybrid against manual logging, and surface uncertainty/user correction.
